text: Weighing trade-offs: cost, latency, quality, and maintainability. The last lesson compared two options, one axis at a time. Most real architecture decisions involve more than two options and more than one axis at once -- this lesson covers a simple, honest technique for making that kind of multi-criteria decision explicit, and just as important, its real limits.

Suppose three vector database candidates each look strong on a different dimension. Option A is cheapest but has middling latency and quality. Option B has excellent latency and quality but costs more. Option C is balanced across every dimension without excelling at any one. 'Which is best' has no single honest answer stated that way -- the real question is 'best for what we actually care about, weighted the way we actually care about it.'

That's the weighted scoring matrix. Score each option one to ten on each relevant criterion, assign a weight to each criterion reflecting its relative importance, with weights summing to one, and compute each option's weighted total. Weighting cost most heavily because the team is cost-sensitive at its current scale, option A edges out the other two -- but notice how close all three scores are, seven-ten, six-ninety, and seven-oh.

That closeness is itself an important, honest result. The scoring step -- how good is each option at cost, at latency -- is usually the easy, relatively objective part. The weights -- how much you care about cost relative to latency relative to maintainability -- are where the actual judgment call lives, and they deserve at least as much explicit discussion as the final answer. Two engineers can agree on every individual score and still recommend a different option, purely because they weighted things differently.

When the top two options are close, as A and C are here, it's worth running a sensitivity check: how much would the weights have to change before the ranking flips? If a small shift flips the recommendation, that's valuable information -- the decision is genuinely close and worth a real conversation about priorities. If the ranking is robust to small changes, that's useful too -- it means the decision is more solid than it might feel.

A weighted scoring matrix doesn't remove the judgment call -- it makes the judgment call visible and debatable instead of hidden inside a gut feeling. Next up: writing a design document that actually gets approved, where this kind of scoring becomes part of the case you make to reviewers.
